scores.accuracy_concern: Rests on a single small 1998 study (27 women with mild to moderate stress leakage, laboratory cough test); check that it was randomised as described; the absent correlation with strength is a non-significant finding, not evidence that strength is irrelevant.
scores.sharpen: Say 'in a small 1998 study of 27 women' in the caption and pair the squeeze with a clear pointer to supervised pelvic floor training for at least 3 months, so one technique is not presented as the whole treatment.

scores.values_concern: Frame the gap at commissioning and system level so it does not read as criticism of continence nurses.
scores.accuracy_concern: NICE NG123 covers women only; the pads-are-not-treatment wording must be quoted exactly and paired with CG97 for men; the claim that services report products supplied rather than outcomes is unsourced and should be dropped.
scores.sharpen: Open on the recognisable contrast (a pad size is recorded, a cause is not) rather than 'NICE describes', and attribute the standard to NG123 for women and CG97 for men.

scores.accuracy_concern: Toilet count and key price change and rest on scheme websites that may not be openable from this environment; 'RADAR key' is the older name; the Yip 2013 isolation link is cross-sectional and says nothing about whether the key helps.
scores.sharpen: Verify the toilet count and key price from an opened source or drop the number, and add one line pointing to a GP or continence service for the urgency itself.

scores.accuracy_concern: Median and mean reductions in leaks do not give the proportion of people still leaking; use the cure proportions the trials report; Resnick 1985 reference details are unconfirmed.
scores.sharpen: Give it a concrete opening and report cure proportions from the trials rather than inferring them from median reductions, or fold its message into C12-20 or C12-32.

scores.accuracy_concern: The Meddings halving of catheter infections came from hospital inpatient studies and should not be applied to discharge or community care; the claim that people leave hospital without a removal plan has no UK source yet.
scores.sharpen: Keep the three-field tag but present the 'halved infections' figure as inpatient evidence only, and say who removes the catheter or runs the trial without it in a care home or at home.

scores.accuracy_concern: Duration of furosemide effect varies by source and product (roughly 4 to 8 hours); evidence that people skip diuretics for outings is unconfirmed; SmPC and BNF pages may not be openable here.
scores.sharpen: Anchor the timing claim to the SmPC or BNF figure actually opened, and find one study showing people skip or delay diuretics for outings, or keep it as a question to ask without that claim.

scores.accuracy_concern: 'Bladder tablets' overgeneralises: the dry-mouth link is with antimuscarinics, and mirabegron causes much less; Tan 2018 pooled heterogeneous intervention studies; the industry-authored Wagg persistence study is off-topic here.
scores.sharpen: Say 'antimuscarinic bladder tablets' rather than 'bladder tablets', and close on a concrete review question such as 'Has anyone asked about your mouth since this tablet started?'

scores.accuracy_concern: Thom 1997 figures are adjusted relative risks from a 1990s US HMO cohort; they show an association and do not show that treating incontinence prevents a move; the 'harder than behavioural symptoms' claim needs its primary source.
scores.sharpen: Keep 'a care home can still be the right choice' prominent and state the Thom figures as an association from an older US cohort, not as evidence that treatment prevents admission.

scores.values_concern: Avoid implying nurses choose pads for convenience; name staffing and call-bell response as the conditions that shape the default.
scores.accuracy_concern: One Israeli cohort with self-reported incontinence at discharge; sicker, less mobile patients are more likely to receive pads or catheters, so the odds ratios are associations open to confounding; the claim about documentation reflecting products is unsourced.
scores.sharpen: Say in the post that sicker people are more likely to get pads or catheters, so the study shows a link and not proof of cause, and frame the fix as help to the toilet and answered call bells.

scores.accuracy_concern: The stated reason for the Pharmacy First age limit is inferred rather than sourced; age boundaries differ between England (16 to 64) and Scotland and must be checked; the symptom checklist and 'poor guides' panel repeat C12-17.
scores.sharpen: Fold the pharmacy age-limit hook into C12-17 as one line, or drop it; if kept, source the reason for the age limit instead of inferring it.

scores.accuracy_concern: 'Leaks often come from one broken link' is unquantified; the Brown 2000 falls link is an association and the rushing mechanism was the authors' hypothesis.
scores.sharpen: Add the night-time version of the chain (light, commode, urinal bottle) and one sourced sentence defining functional incontinence so the post rests on more than common sense.

scores.accuracy_concern: Retention near death from opioids and anticholinergic medicines needs a palliative care guideline source; HOUDINI publication details are unconfirmed; coordinate with C19 to avoid a cross-category repeat.
scores.sharpen: Open with the concrete situation (turns for pad changes are painful in the last days) and cite one UK palliative care guideline beside the CDC indication.

scores.accuracy_concern: Johanson 1996 and Talbot 1995 are old US samples, not older inpatients; the claim that softer wording ('leak' rather than 'incontinent') changes answers is unsupported.
scores.sharpen: Find support for the wording point or drop it, and tie each question to one ward action so the card is more than a reminder to ask.

scores.accuracy_concern: Blockage frequency and the 'spare catheter at home' advice need a source, as local practice varies; the first-check steps must match NHS or RCN wording exactly.
scores.sharpen: Check the first steps against RCN or NHS wording, add NHS 111 as the fallback number, and make clear that carers are not expected to change the catheter themselves.

scores.accuracy_concern: Small 1990s US nursing home studies with older continence products; the 87% figure is unverified; 'no worse skin' comes from one small controlled study; C11 may cover night checks too.
scores.sharpen: State the study era and setting on the post and visual, verify the 9 in 10 figure, and suggest a one-week count of night wakes a care home could run itself.

scores.accuracy_concern: A 1995 US research cohort with research staff delivering prompts; responder rates may not hold in routine care; 'a new resident's first weeks' is the post's inference, not a finding; the 41% and wet-check figures need checking.
scores.sharpen: Present the first weeks after admission as a suggestion rather than a finding, and name the staff time prompted voiding needs so the post does not imply it is free.

scores.accuracy_concern: Midthun 2004 is small (97 pads) and the 'about a third wrong' figure needs checking; UKHSA over-65 wording should be quoted exactly.
scores.sharpen: Keep the named-belief opening, quote UKHSA wording exactly, and add one line on what antibiotics for harmless bacteria cost the person (side effects, C. difficile, resistance).

scores.accuracy_concern: The flow must include all UKHSA over-65 signs (including new or worse confusion and rigors) or it misstates the guidance; dipstick advice differs for people with catheters; Crellin 2018 is observational.
scores.sharpen: Put the full UKHSA over-65 sign list in the flow, keep the trimethoprim harm as an absolute excess in people on RAS blockers or spironolactone, and differentiate clearly from C12-17.

scores.accuracy_concern: The two-cause frame omits infection, including C. difficile, and medicines such as antibiotics, as causes of new loose stool in frail older people.
scores.sharpen: Add a third branch for infection (new diarrhoea needs a stool sample, including for C. difficile) so the teaching card does not miss the dangerous cause.

scores.accuracy_concern: The Burgio intervention was biofeedback-assisted behavioural treatment (pelvic floor training and urge control), not bladder training as NICE defines it; the drug was immediate-release oxybutynin; the persistence data are industry-authored.
scores.sharpen: Call the intervention 'behavioural treatment with pelvic floor training and urge control' rather than 'bladder training', and put the trial exclusions (no dementia, walking unaided) on the chart.

scores.accuracy_concern: Urge suppression was one component of multicomponent programmes and its separate effect has not been tested; the falls link is an association only.
scores.sharpen: Say the stop-and-squeeze step is one part of a programme that works, and pair it with a next step such as a bladder diary or a continence nurse.

scores.accuracy_concern: Cochrane evidence for vaginal oestrogen rests on two small trials; the over-the-counter 10 microgram tablet is licensed for vaginal dryness, not urine infection prevention; that women decline it fearing HRT risks is an unsourced assumption.
scores.sharpen: Make clear the over-the-counter product is for vaginal dryness, not urine infections, and give the Cochrane result as 'fewer infections in two small trials'.

scores.accuracy_concern: The institutional result has wide uncertainty (RR 0.93, 0.67 to 1.30) and its certainty grade needs checking; do not assert that care homes routinely give cranberry without a source.
scores.sharpen: Show the institutional result with its uncertainty in plain words ('did not show a clear benefit') and add absolute numbers per 100 from the summary of findings tables.

scores.accuracy_concern: The composite outcome was driven mainly by bacteriuria, the unadjusted difference was not significant, and the trial was small (75 men); 'fewer infections or deaths' overclaims.
scores.sharpen: Describe the outcome as mostly bacteria in the urine rather than 'fewer infections or deaths', and put sizing and daily skin checks on the visual.

scores.accuracy_concern: Heaton 1992 sampled adults aged about 25 to 69, not older people; the three-a-day to three-a-week range comes from earlier work (Connell 1965); NICE lower gastrointestinal referral now relies on FIT testing.
scores.sharpen: State the age range of the Bristol sample, attribute the frequency range to its source, and align the 'see your GP' box with current NICE wording.

scores.accuracy_concern: Johanson 1996 was a 1990s US clinic sample of adults of all ages; 'most never tell a doctor' should read 'in one US survey, about 2 in 3 had not'.
scores.sharpen: Give the one-third figure with its source and era, and end with what a GP or continence service can offer so the reader knows what to expect.

scores.accuracy_concern: Evidence is mainly expert consensus; moisture and pressure damage can coexist, and superficial sacral damage may be either; the GLOBIAD citation is unconfirmed.
scores.sharpen: Add that the two can coexist and uncertain cases need a nurse's assessment, and cite the GLOBIAD tool or IAD consensus explicitly.

scores.accuracy_concern: Booster pads without a waterproof backing are designed to be layered; the claim that layering makes leaks and sore skin more likely rests on service advice rather than studies.
scores.sharpen: Exclude booster pads designed for layering, and find a published continence service or consensus source before asserting that double padding worsens leaks and skin.

scores.accuracy_concern: The CDC guideline is US and its full text has not been opened; the Meddings halving applies to inpatient studies; 'one-point restraint' is an editorial term, not a finding; overlaps C12-05 on reason and removal plan.
scores.sharpen: Merge with C12-05, or differentiate by focusing on nurse-led removal protocols and UK guidance, with the CDC list translated into UK terms.

scores.accuracy_concern: ICS thresholds differ between the 2002 and 2019 reports; two patterns simplify mixed nocturia and sleep-driven waking; NICE CG97 applies to men; nocturia is in C11's scope.
scores.sharpen: Coordinate with C11 to avoid a repeat, allow for mixed patterns, and use the threshold from the current ICS terminology report.

scores.accuracy_concern: Harms of fluid restriction (constipation, dizziness, bladder irritation from concentrated urine) are weakly supported; Talbot 1995 is small and old; NG123 applies to women; overlaps C13 hydration.
scores.sharpen: Keep to NICE wording on modifying high or low fluid intake and trying less caffeine, and drop the weakly supported harms.

scores.accuracy_concern: A non-inferiority result, not superiority; trial in Canadian community-dwelling women without cognitive impairment, with physiotherapist-led groups; the week-4 figure comes from a 2025 secondary analysis and needs checking.
scores.sharpen: Say 'reduced leaks about as much', give the medians in plain words, and note the trial setting and that groups were led by physiotherapists.

scores.accuracy_concern: Post-micturition dribble is common and usually harmless and must be distinguished from continuous leakage; NICE CG97 wording on measuring residual volume before antimuscarinics needs checking; residual thresholds vary.
scores.sharpen: Distinguish continuous leakage from the common after-dribble, and check the NICE CG97 wording on residual volume before any bladder tablet.

scores.accuracy_concern: Footstool evidence is from small studies, mostly in younger adults; the bedpan claim has no source; early-morning timing comes from a 25 to 69 population sample.
scores.sharpen: Drop or source the bedpan claim, and label the footstool evidence as small studies so the practical advice is not oversold.

scores.accuracy_concern: Toilet count and the scope of the England building regulation rest on web sources that may not be openable here; campaign surveys are not independent evidence.
scores.sharpen: Verify the count from an opened source or omit it, state the building regulation scope precisely, and tie the post to older people who need a hoist after stroke or in advanced illness.

scores.accuracy_concern: TOPSY was a superiority trial that found no clear difference in quality of life, so 'did as well as' overstates; about half responded at 4 years.
scores.sharpen: Replace 'did as well as' with 'showed no clear difference in quality of life', and keep the trial exclusions on slide 3.

scores.accuracy_concern: Gill 2005 shows increased dispensing (an association) that could partly reflect dementia progression or closer contact with prescribers; the absolute difference (4.5% vs 3.1%) should be given; the SmPC frequency category needs checking.
scores.sharpen: Give the absolute figures (about 4 or 5 in 100 vs 3 in 100) and coordinate with C06 so the prescribing cascade is not posted twice.

scores.values_concern: Avoid implying care staff give up on people with dementia; frame pads-first as a service pattern and keep the person's dignity central.
scores.accuracy_concern: 'Several of the best trials excluded dementia' needs a count and names; 'often moved straight to pads' needs support beyond a small qualitative study (Drennan 2011).
scores.sharpen: Replace 'several' with a named count of trials that excluded people with dementia, and use a stronger opening than a statement about an evidence gap.

allocation_reason: 36 of 38 candidates reach about 36 and 19 reach 44 or more with no disqualifying flag (the stated formula's true maximum is 55, not 50), and continence is almost untouched by the earlier collection, so the category supports the maximum even after folding C12-10 into C12-17 and C12-29 into C12-05.
balance_note: The top 14 split well by audience (5 practitioners: C12-09, C12-18, C12-05, C12-19, C12-33; 4 public: C12-08, C12-22, C12-36, C12-03; 5 both: C12-23, C12-17, C12-11, C12-32, C12-20), but by topic they lean towards women (C12-20, C12-22, C12-32, C12-36) and urine infection (C12-17, C12-18, C12-22, C12-23), with only one bowel post (C12-19) and one men's post (C12-33). Consider swapping C12-20 or C12-32 for C12-26 (bowel leakage, public) and adding C12-16 or C12-15 for care homes; the Who gets left out series has no entry in the top 14 (C12-38 is the best candidate for it).
notes: Cross-category overlaps to coordinate: C12-12 with C19 (palliative care), C12-30 and C12-15 with C11 (nocturia and night checks), C12-37 with C06 (prescribing cascades), C12-07 and C12-31 with C13 (mouth care, hydration). No candidate takes delirium as its topic; C12-18 must still list new or worse confusion as one UKHSA sign to state the guidance accurately.
